I loathe this game.

THE STORY:
Terrible. One of the worst stories in any Monster Hunter game, if not any game. I'm constantly surrounded by the Burger King Kids Club for every single aspect of my journey. Every decision is a melodramatic therapy session to appease a 12-year-old boy who fell in love with the monster who tried murdering him and his people. Everything you do is commented on by your insufferable followers. Health low? "Hey, Hunter! Drink a potion!". Ran out of food buff? "Hey, Hunter, we have food ingredients!". And it NEVER ends. Why do Palicos talk now? Why do I even need the obnoxious quirk-chungus handler following me 24/7 telling ME when I'm allowed to hunt? Why does every decision revolve around a 12-year-old boy and his ridiculous emotional whims? Why is this game not even about ME and my accomplishments hunting monsters? Have we forgotten the original soul of Monster Hunter? The sheer might of a hunter felling a Rathalos either alone or with other (human player) hunters while Wagnerian trumpets blare in the background at your accomplishments. Where has that gone? (Watch the intro to Monster Hunter 1 on the PS2 to understand what I mean). This game is a perfect example of how a series has plummeted from its hardcore origins to appease people who forget to breathe.

GAMEPLAY:
This is still somewhat enjoyable, but I still feel it's lacking. It doesn't seem like much of the action has evolved from MH World. Nor did this game take any notes from the wonderful action of MH Rise with its intensity - some of the best in the series. There's a new expansion for Wilds coming out which addresses some of these issues, but I remain skeptical. If anything, the game feels more forgiving than previous titles when fighting monsters. I can't quite put my finger on all of it, but everything feels "safe" and "slower". Like previous titles, you also have a Palico following you around giving heals and debuffs, and helping attack the monster - I personally never liked this, but it's been with us since Freedom Unite (2008). You also have many world objects which can aid in the battle. So there is an overabundance of hand-holding, and I only found myself dying twice during the entire main story playthrough. It took everything wrong with World and amplified it, as well as removing the things which made World unique and fun. More obnoxious story and more obnoxious handler which NO ONE asked for. Removed player housing which served as a fun aspect to World where we could catch our endemic life pets and display them in our rooms. Catching endemic life serves very little purpose now other than fulfilling annoying side quests. Fishing is the same and has gotten worse. There is no longer 1 central hub that caters to everything you need. You have to hop from one small crappy town to the next to get things like gem melding or bigger food buffs. MH World had a perfect hub that made it easy to access other areas via hook transport; now you have to fiddle with the new awful map to journey to another area. "Oh, but we get to control and ride a mount now!" you say. WHO CARES. This was never necessary, and the controls for the Seikret are terrible. Sometimes the damned thing just refuses to jump off a cliff because you have to be in a very exact location for it to register. I never thought I'd be saying the fast travel mounts in World would be something I'd miss, but here we are. All in all, many aspects of the gameplay seem to be rushed. Half-baked ideas that were never fully fleshed out. Many missing features from World, yet asking for a higher price tag. More ridiculous cash-grab DLC. How greedy and incompetent Capcom has become.

GRAPHICS:
This is the bulk of negative reviews you will see. Honestly, this area is my least concern about the game because the things I mentioned above are way more problematic. You can't get away from this without talking about "optimization". Yes, the game runs like crap, and is generally ugly to look at. I don't like any of the areas and they are all an artistic devolution compared to World and Rise and run much worse. I have no connection to any of this and I generally did not care about exploring because of the blandness and ugliness of it all. Your starting hub looks like you took a Detroit hobo enclave shoved into the New Mexico desert. I cannot think of anything more uninspiring and dreadful than going there after a quest. The game itself runs better than it initially did with the demo. They did improve some things here and there, but it's still rough. People, including me, still get crashes. Crashes that restart your PC, making you have to do the quest again. My PC (which I built) is generally very good and I make sure cooling and temps are always at optimal levels. Needless to say, I don't have this issue much with any other games. The game generally runs well for me today (~60 fps, 1080p), all things aside. It could be better, considering how low fidelity it is.

CONCLUSION:
If you are new to the series, just buy World and stay away from this. Want more Monster Hunter without any fluff? Buy Rise. Wilds is a downgrade in many ways to previous titles. Do not buy this expecting Ascendance (the new expansion) will fix all these problems - it won't. In fact, it may compound them.

ME:
Monster Hunter is my favorite game series of all time. I main as Hammer, and do a bit of Hunting Horn on the side. I've been playing since Freedom Unite (2008). I eventually went back and cleared the original PS2 game (2004) on its story mode. I went on to play the Japanese PSP title Portable 3rd (incredible). I also put considerable time into Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate, 4 Ultimate - both for the 3DS, and the most time I've spent was with World, and also a bit of time in Rise. All of these games I enjoyed and put hundreds of hours into and found it interesting how the series evolved from its clunky origins to the fast-paced action it is today. It saddens me greatly what this series has become, and there is no going back. I'm hopeful other companies will make quality monster-hunting games of their own that compete with this garbage we've been handed.

Wilds is an overall really good Monster Hunter game that's had some consistent annoyances holding it back for a decent amount of its lifespan. Note that this review reflects only the base game, not Ascendance (since it's not out yet). I would recommend it, but with some caveats.
The gameplay is classic MonHun, with some new flourishes from the post-World era mixed in with some classic mechanics returning after being missing in Rise. Initially, the game was presented as semi-open world, but I think that this system is so insignificant that it should just be removed; the maps just feel like normal MonHun minus a suspiciously long hallway between areas (which should just be a loading screen)... 
The loop of prepping gear, exploring a map, hunting a monster and carving is just as satisfying as it ever was. The monsters are all really great fights, with some very memorable newcomers and returning favorites (and Blagonga. I don't like the poop monkey). Solo play is very nice, and I'm glad they picked up a lot from Rise when implementing helpers and other similar systems. Joining friends unfortunately goes back to the World-style lobby system, so it can be frustrating to juggle the odd menus (I'd much prefer the old-school system, but Capcom insists on treating lobbies like a pseudo-MMO space, so whatever). At least you're no longer locked behind cutscenes when playing with friends, so that's nice. 
Visually the game CAN look fantastic, with some caveats. To address the elephant in the room; the game runs somewhat poorly. It USED to run ABYSMALLY on anything but the highest-end hardware, but they've since done a lot of optimizations and changes to try and smooth things out (really wish they'd remove their dysfunctional anti-tamper system which bogs down performance and doesn't work, but Capcom's taken an aggressive stance on mods in recent years, so I don't expect this to change). The game can now even run decently on a Switch 2, so they've certainly fixed it for the most part; although I think that the game frankly doesn't look much better than World for worse performance. The game has a dynamic weather and time system, which means that sometimes the maps are fully lit and gorgeous, and sometimes they're overcast and bland; which sucks because man, do the pretty moments look PRETTY.
Despite these issues, this game is very good overall. Fun MonHun, what can I say. It's even cheaper now forever than it was before, so (if your computer can handle it) please try it out.

In its current state, I cannot recommend Monster Hunter Wilds to anyone, existing fan or new player. I've been playing Monster Hunter for ~13 years now and every time I try to boot up Wilds to give it another shot I regret doing so. You'd be much better off playing any of the other games in the series. The game runs poorly, even on decent hardware, and the gameplay is a total cakewalk until sudden difficulty spikes with endgame Title Update content. The current endgame is a complete disaster with RNG thrown into quite literally every aspect of set building, with not only RNG talismans and RNG decorations, but even gacha rolling for stats and skills on the Gogma weapons. Booting up Wilds is an exercise in miserable frustration as I realize all that matters is farming the same two or three fights endlessly so that I can shovel more materials into the set building gacha. I have some much more subjective complaints with the design of a lot of the endgame fights, but I genuinely cannot believe that the latest entry in my favorite video game series of all time makes me this bored out of my mind. The Ascension expansion is right around the corner and could very well fix a lot of these issues, so if you are on the fence about buying Wilds, I would *highly* recommend you avoid it for now and go play literally any other Monster Hunter game.

I will leave this overall pessimistic rant with one positive point- the endgame of base Rise was downright awful and then Sunbreak turned it around into one of my all-time favorite Monster Hunter games, so there is definitely still time for Wilds to turn around.

I completely understand that MH elitists will not welcome this new design ethos but I think it's the way forward for this franchise, at least for the mainline games. It's very possible that the portable games will retain the hallmarks of the older games which would be the perfect compromise.

Hunts are wicked fast. Even in high rank, you'll rarely be in a hunt for longer than 15 minutes. This isn't something I envisioned that I'd enjoy, but after doing hundreds of hunts in Wilds, it's amazing. There is virtually no downtime within hunts themselves. Locating and chasing monsters is quite literally, automatic. Healing and stabilizing status ailments is much faster, and carries far less risk. There is no more dang monster tracking except for trace amounts in the campaign and monster crowns can be checked for before starting a hunt. There are no siege missions, defense missions, or gimmick fights. You simply hunt monsters. Best of all, hunts seamlessly flow between each other with zero downtime. The open-world nature of this game suits Monster Hunter perfectly and Capcom pulled it off with their first attempt. Even your eating buffs are retained between hunts - it's really awesome.

I love each and every one of these changes among so many others, and it's going to be a serious struggle for me to go back to any of the previous games. The obvious drawback here is that the game is made much easier overall. I can live with this, the game is considerably more enjoyable for me as a direct consequence and there is still real challenge to be found in the endgame for those who get that far.

Master rank in Ascendance is going to be a treat, especially since it'll invariably raise the difficulty to a level more in line with previous games. Until then, I'll be getting the gold and miniature crowns for every monster because it's just so much fun to do.

Monster Hunter Wilds is worse than some people expected, but apparently that’s enough to declare the entire franchise a disaster. Regarding the Insect Glaive (IG)

I know a lot of people have issues with the key bindings; I changed a few keys and managed to play through the whole game, but the weapon does have one major flaw.

Why does the aerial playstyle deal no damage? Why is it limited to just a repositioning tool? Dual Blades can dodge, Why can't IG capitalize on its rapid, three-dimensional movement to weave in and out of combat with the monster? Stamina management is identical to "Demon Mode," except that instead of toggling it on and off, you're switching between the ground and the air.

Why are there no aerial good play style?

Compared to MH Rise, aerial gameplay has been completely sidelined. The "Diving Wyvern" has been replaced by the "Rising Spiral Slash" as a high-damage attack, "Jumping Slash" remains the same (good old helicopter), But why wasn't "Kinsect Slash" included as a move in Focus Mode?

Aerial focused builds are not gonna be optimal damage-wise for a lot of reasons. First of all, the main way to boost your damage in this game comes from increasing your crit rate (affinity) and your crit damage, and of the 3 main skills we use for that two of them cannot really be used for aerial attacks: Maximum Might because you’re never gonna be close to full stamina, and Weakness Exploit because you’re unlikely to hit weak spots up in the air except on already wounded parts. The second reason is that the motion values and elemental modifiers on aerial attacks are pretty terrible compared with your ground attacks, even with the buffs on repeated bounces. And finally it’s very easy to get slapped off the air by any of the huge vertical hitboxes of many monsters’ attacks before you even get to touch them.

It’s very obvious that in Wilds (like in most of the previous titles) IG was designed to be played mostly on the ground, and that its aerial moveset was not meant as a damage tool, but mainly as a way to reposition and dodge; indeed, in the Beta they even geared down a lot of the aerial stuff that was added since Monster Hunter World, and they only added it back after people complained about it, but without really caring to make it particularly strong or competitive. For this reason, I recommend to newer players that want to learn to play the weapon optimally to try to ignore the aerial part of its toolkit as much as possible and to play it as a normal weapon but with the additional upside of being able to close the gap quickly or to jump over attacks that are otherwise hard to dodge. If you do that, you’ll have access to what is probably one of the top 3 strongest weapons in the game; if you don’t, it’s likely gonna be bottom 1.

If anyone ever wants to play this weapon, I highly recommend playing MH Rise; I hope the developers change their minds and take inspiration from Rise's balancing to bring back the Insect Glaive.

Let's see if the DLC fixes this weapon.

Playstyle wise this is a fitting successor to World, similar enough that it's easy to jump to while featuring QOL reworks to the slinger, weapons, and the addition of wounding.     While not something most players think about the sound design stands out to me much in the way it caught my attention in World; Rey Dau has very digitized calls while still feeling organic, and Arkveld's roar is almost mechanical in a way that adds to the feel of it being a more primeval monster. More fantastic sound direction that gives genuine consideration to distinct vocalizations.
    Character creation surprised me with how unexpectedly immaculate the face blending is; really I cannot overstate how elated I was to go into it with an established character - and thus very specific facial structure - in mind and get within a hair's breadth of 1:1 on model. Fully voiced hunter was also a pleasant surprise, though I would have liked a couple more base options as the pitch filter starts adding that digitized glaze to the sound after a couple of notches down. My sole complaint on cc is I want the loose pompadour from Iceborne back, which I would gladly still pay for if it’s independent DLC.

    Wilds has been unfairly review bombed and treated as The Game To Dump On For Clout, and this undoubtedly has made the optimization team's jobs harder. If you [i]actually[/i] read the patch notes you’ll find [i]all[/i] major updates had attempts at addressing the stability concerns. No perceptible improvement to you ≠ not being worked on. Cosmetic DLC releases and small patches ≠ not being worked on. TU2 included backend tweaks with Steam regarding asset load, and this one actually made the game run mildly [i]worse[/i] on my rig with longer model and texture load times.
    It probably took so long for one of these updates to make a meaningful difference because “runs terribly on my 4070” is not usable for troubleshooting. The full specs of your hardware matter; they don't have access to every single possible hardware combination to test on and rely on user reports containing enough information to find a common denominator between them. I can only imagine the number of ultimately unusable reports they had to filter through given the changes made to in game crash reports that preceded TU4 - expanding the data collected and sent back. Not to mention they started essentially begging players to mind their GPU drivers because the devs can't fix crashing that's caused by your installed drivers.

    For the record I’ve been running it just fine on a 3060 since midnight on launch day, only [i]one[/i] crash and one mesh wig out in 900+ hours I put in prior to TU4. I had negligible frame loss and slow loading assets but “unplayable” it was not.

Out of all the action games on the market, the Monster Hunter series has the most complex weapon movesets and in depth combo systems and Monster Hunter Wilds is no exception to this. While the complexity of the weapons can make it seem difficult to approach for new players, Wilds has the best gradual difficulty progression and weapon maneuverability in the entire franchise, making it one of the best new player friendly Monster Hunter games. With 14 different weapons and different ways to play each weapon, you can try out different playstyles to find the one that suits you the best. Every weapon also has an extremely high skill ceiling, so players who enjoy optimizing damage and self improvement can find themselves sinking tons of time into the game. 

The main drawback with the game and where most of the negative reception results from is due to expensive hardware requirements, graphical complaints with low quality textures, and performance issues especially with PCs closer or under the recommended requirement threshold. While Capcom has taken a few steps to address the technical issues of the game since launch, it remains to be an issue for players with lower end PCs, especially with those who have specs closer to the minimum requirements.

However, if you own a PC that is well above the recommended requirements and can perform well on the technical side, Monster Hunter Wilds is a game that is well worth its high price for anyone who enjoys action games considering the amount time that you can get out of it, weapon complexity, monster variety, and its attention to detail.

Might have a few issues on the technical side and with the early game design decisions.
But when I'm dashing through the air with an insect glaive or discerning dodging out of the way of a massive dragon beam, not too many games can beat that experience.
A worthy inclusion to the Monster Hunter series and I hope Capcom can refine it further with the upcoming DLC.

Review after completing a majority of the content - up to Gogmazios.  May update this review after the Ascendance expansion comes out.

[b]TLDR:[/b]  It's a good game, but it has some issues.  The core gameplay is still that delightful Monster Hunter formula.  The open world isn't as open as I thought it would be.  Story is cringier than World.  There are some strange design decisions.  I hate Arch Tempered Arkveld.   

[h1]The Good:[/h1]
- If you're looking for that hit of that Monster Hunting goodness with a change of scenery and a small twist on the combat formula, this game will provide that for you.  The core combat doesn't get old (even if most of the monsters do).  Learning how to master a weapon and taking that knowledge and skill to fight against giant monsters is just plain fun.
- Some interesting new ideas for environments, and some great new monster designs. The "living world" or real-time rotations of monsters leading into procedurally generated field missions is a cool idea.
- Weapon and armor designs are top-notch
- I fight Rey Dau over and over again just to listen to their theme music.

[h1]The Bad:[/h1]
- This is a game that was not built specifically for PC, and it shows.  There's this very odd blend of high and low resolution textures in and around the maps that threw me off for awhile  I thought it was a rendering issue at first until I looked it up.  Likely a compromise to get the game to run more smoothly.  I am playing the game on a pretty powerful PC - and even at highest settings with no DLSS some things looked odd and low-poly.  In terms of performance issues, I didn't have any - but I know I definitely would have some if I tried to download and play this game on my much less powerful laptop.
- They put some weird filtering over the environments, which I think makes them look more drab and boring (even if they probably look more realistic that way)
- The story of the game is some of the cringiest S**T I have ever heard.  Being a game from Japan, I always expect a certain level of "anime cringe" from the dialogue - it's basically it's own cultural thing, and when done well it can be entertaining. But my goodness, this story is a step down from World's story.  Monster Hunter World really leaned into the campiness of their story, but it worked out much better because the themes of that game were really focused around adventure and exploration.  Wild's story is a character drama, and it's a poorly written one.  I ended up skipping most of the dialogue and cutscenes because it was boring and uncomfortable.
- There's a few absolute banger songs and themes, but the soundtrack for the most part felt quite lackluster.  Made fighting enemies less interesting.
- This game is an MMO-lite, so it expects you to grind to get materials for gear. Back when I played World, I had the luxury of being able to sink a lot of time into it.  Nowadays, that's far less likely to happen. Expect to sink hours into the game while trying to acquire the materials you need for that piece of gear you really want to make or upgrade.  (I used mods to streamline this process, which is partly why this playthrough is only around ~40 hours)
- Just like previous games, navigating through the menus is still kind of rough. It takes some getting used to.
- I hate Arch Tempered Arkveld. All my homies hate Arch Tempered Arkveld.  Get off me with that constant attack-spam BS.

[h1] World vs Wilds [/h1]
The debate rages on!  In my personal opinion - World is the better game.  Something about World just fits the idea of Monster Hunter better for me. The setting, music, story were all things I could latch onto more easily.  World still looks gorgeous despite its age, and I prefer the more condensed map designs. They really made the most of their limitations and it shows. It also runs great on current gen hardware.  

If you have a lower end PC and are looking to get into Monster Hunter, World is what you should buy.  It's usually on sale for pretty cheap too.  If you want to stay current - Wilds is a solid choice if your computer can handle it and you're willing to fork over some more cash. 

It's possible that the upcoming Ascendance expansion will change things in the game enough that I develop a more positive opinion on it. [b]For now though - I'd put it at a solid 7 or 7.5/10.[/b]

It's fun for a while once you figure out how to tune decent performance out of it, and there are some notable QoL improvements over previous entries, but there are some glaring issues as well.

Many of the late-game monsters have the ability to one-shot you, even with upgraded armor and defensive decorations.  They also have the ability to stun-lock you without actually stunning you, and then hitting you while you're down (something they could not do in previous games) or timing their moves to hit you exactly when you get up, making them unavoidable.  A lot of the late-game difficulty seems to derive from either one-shotting the player with moves that can't be avoided or by speeding up the monster's attacks so there is no gap in between their massive sweeping AOE moves.  Since the player characters tend to be quite slow, this is another spot where attacks often become unavoidable.  These design choices are to the game's detriment.  I'm not a fan of unavoidable deaths in games, particularly when that's the main source of the game's difficulty.

The biggest problem I have is the completely buggy hit detection.  I'm constantly getting nailed by attacks that I either clearly dodged out of, or that did not even remotely connect in the first place.  It becomes a real problem when stronger monsters start getting one-hit kills on you when they attack the opposite direction from you.  It's unfortunate, but that issue in particular prevents the game from getting my recommendation until it's fixed.
